label: Title
notes: Open by naming the problem: set polarity already turns a convex body into the inequalities that test it, and this section asks what the same move does to functions. Preview the two routes: gauges behave like unit balls, while general nonnegative convex functions require epigraph polarity and a reflected vertical coordinate.

label: Set Polarity To Epigraphs
notes: Start from the picture rather than the formula. A convex function is represented by its epigraph, so polarizing functions means polarizing an epigraph in one dimension higher. The vertical reflection is the small but important bookkeeping step that turns the polar cone back into an epigraph.

label: Polar Function Definition
notes: Give students the definition as an inequality machine. For a proposed value mu star, every primal point must satisfy the displayed bound. The polar value is the smallest such multiplier, and for a gauge the additive one disappears because positive homogeneity lets the inequality be rescaled.

label: Gauge And Support Pair
notes: Use the unit ball as the anchor. The gauge asks how far one must dilate C to catch x; the polar gauge asks how large the pairing can be on C. This is why a gauge and the support function of its unit set form the basic polar pair.

label: Indicator And Support Examples
notes: This slide is meant to reduce the abstraction. Indicators remember membership, gauges remember scaling, and support functions remember the farthest exposed value. Polarity moves among those viewpoints, so the same convex set can be read as a feasible region, a unit ball, or a family of tests.

label: Quadratic And Norm Examples
notes: Emphasize that the familiar inequalities are not side examples; they are model cases of polar gauges. The Euclidean norm is self-polar, the max norm pairs with the one norm, lp pairs with lq, and an ellipsoid polar inverts the positive definite matrix.

label: Order Reversal
notes: Make the order reversal concrete. If f is below g, then epi f is larger than epi g, and larger sets have smaller polars. After returning to function order, the polar of f sits above the polar of g. This is the same reversal students saw for polar sets.

label: Bipolar Recovery
notes: Connect the theorem directly to closure. The first polar keeps exactly the inequalities visible from the epigraph; the second polar reconstructs the closed convex epigraph those inequalities determine. Closed functions are recovered exactly, while nonclosed functions return with their epigraph boundary filled in.

label: Scaling And Operations
notes: Treat this as an operations ledger, not a full algebra. Positive vertical scaling inverts under polarity, order reverses, and set gauges inherit the usual polar-set calculus. Warn that pointwise sums or maxima do not have a one-line polar rule unless the corresponding epigraph operation is tracked.

label: Domain And Positivity Caveats
notes: Pause on hypotheses before examples hide them. The extended polar in this section is designed for nonnegative convex functions that vanish at the origin. Gauges add positive homogeneity. If a function is not closed, the bipolar recovers its closure, and if the positivity normalization fails the epigraph-polar formula is not the same transform.

label: Numerical Polar Lab
notes: Use the lab values as quick sanity checks. The l-infinity and l-one row verifies the dual norm inequality, the quadratic row checks matrix inversion, and the scalar quadratic row shows the extended polar definition by minimizing a quadratic residual over x.

label: Fenchel Comparison
notes: Do not let students merge the conjugate and the polar. Fenchel conjugacy produces the best additive inequality; function polarity produces the best bound with a unit budget and a product term. For a norm, the conjugate is an indicator of the dual ball while the polar is the dual norm itself.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Read this slide as the one-page reference for the section. Each row tells students what object is being polarized, what the result is, and what inspection target justifies the rule. The goal is reliable recognition, not memorizing disconnected formulas.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the epigraph picture. A polar function is a certificate-valued transform: it records the smallest multiplier that makes all pairings valid. Gauges expose support functions, bipolarity recovers closure, and the Fenchel comparison explains why this duality is related to but distinct from conjugacy.
